questions.q: Why does a multi-stage pipeline run build, test, scan, and deploy as separate gated stages instead of one combined step?
options: A failure at any earlier stage should stop the pipeline before wasting time on later, more expensive stages
GitHub Actions technically forbids more than one command per job
Separate stages are required so every stage can run on a different cloud provider
It has no real benefit — it's only done for readability in the YAML file
questions.explain: Staging the pipeline means a build failure never reaches testing, and a test failure never reaches scanning — each gate exists so later, costlier stages don't run against an artifact that already failed an earlier check.

questions.q: What is the key difference between unit tests and integration tests in the test stage?
options: There is no real difference — the terms are interchangeable
Unit tests only check security vulnerabilities, not logic
Unit tests run against code in isolation and run fast; integration tests verify real interaction between components against realistic dependencies
Integration tests run in isolation with no dependencies; unit tests require a live database
questions.explain: Unit tests are fast and isolated; integration tests catch the class of bug that only appears when components actually interact, such as a service calling a real test database or queue.

questions.q: In the scan stage, what does SCA (software composition analysis) check, as distinct from SAST?
options: SCA and SAST both only check Dockerfiles for syntax errors
SCA replaces unit testing entirely
SCA only runs after deploy, never before it
SCA checks third-party and open-source dependencies against known-CVE databases, while SAST analyzes the code your own team wrote
questions.explain: SAST analyzes your own source code for insecure patterns; SCA assumes imported dependencies are a black box and checks their versions against known-vulnerability databases, as covered in the DevSecOps course's scanning chapter.

questions.q: In a GitOps-driven pipeline, what does the `deploy` stage typically do?
options: It SSHes directly into production servers and restarts the application
It updates an image tag or manifest in the GitOps repo, which ArgoCD or Flux then reconciles into the cluster on its own pull-based cycle
It deletes the existing Kubernetes namespace and recreates it from scratch
It skips the GitOps repo entirely and calls the Kubernetes API directly from the CI runner
questions.explain: Consistent with Chapters 3 and 4's GitOps model, the CI pipeline's job ends at making the desired state in Git correct; the GitOps controller's pull-based reconciliation is what actually changes the cluster.

questions.q: In the sample GitHub Actions workflow in this lesson, what does `needs: scan` on the `deploy` job accomplish?
options: It makes `deploy` run in parallel with `scan` to save time
It has no functional effect and is purely documentation
It makes the `deploy` job wait and only start once the `scan` job has completed successfully, enforcing the gate order
It tells GitHub Actions to skip the `scan` job if `deploy` already ran once
questions.explain: `needs:` creates a hard dependency between jobs — `deploy` cannot start until `scan` reports success, which is exactly how the gate chain (build → test → scan → deploy) gets enforced in real YAML.
